title: The Bottle That Looked Like Juice

pages.text: It was a bright spring morning in the village, and Grandma was clearing out her old storeroom. Rose and her little cousin were helping. The storeroom was dark and dusty, and full of things that nobody had touched for years. “Out it all comes,” said Grandma, rolling up her sleeves.
pages.speech: It was a bright spring morning in the village, and Grandma was clearing out her old storeroom. Rose and her little cousin were helping. The storeroom was dark and dusty, and full of things that nobody had touched for years. “Out it all comes,” said Grandma, rolling up her sleeves.

pages.text: They carried out old baskets and cracked flowerpots. They carried out a rusty watering can and a chair with only three legs. The dust made them sneeze, and the sun made them hot. “I’m thirsty,” said Rose’s little cousin, for the third time.
pages.speech: They carried out old baskets and cracked flowerpots. They carried out a rusty watering can and a chair with only three legs. The dust made them sneeze, and the sun made them hot. “I’m thirsty,” said Rose’s little cousin, for the third time.

pages.text: Then he squeezed behind a big box in the corner. “Look,” he called. On the floor stood a bottle full of bright orange liquid. A stripe of sunlight fell on it, and it glowed like a lamp. “Juice!” He reached for the cap.
pages.speech: Then he squeezed behind a big box in the corner. “Look,” he called. On the floor stood a bottle full of bright orange liquid. A stripe of sunlight fell on it, and it glowed like a lamp. “Juice!” He reached for the cap.

pages.text: “Stop!” said Rose, and she caught his hand. “Leave it.” “But I’m thirsty,” he said. His lip wobbled. Rose knelt down beside him. “I know,” she said. “But we don’t touch it. We ask first.”
pages.speech: “Stop!” said Rose, and she caught his hand. “Leave it.” “But I’m thirsty,” he said. His lip wobbled. Rose knelt down beside him. “I know,” she said. “But we don’t touch it. We ask first.”

pages.text: Rose looked at the bottle without touching it. It looked exactly like juice. But who keeps juice in a storeroom, next to the brushes and the bucket, far away from the fridge? The cap was a strange, hard kind of cap. And the label was so faded that Rose couldn’t read it.
pages.speech: Rose looked at the bottle without touching it. It looked exactly like juice. But who keeps juice in a storeroom, next to the brushes and the bucket, far away from the fridge? The cap was a strange, hard kind of cap. And the label was so faded that Rose couldn’t read it.

pages.text: “Grandma,” Rose called. “Please come and look.” Her little cousin held her hand tight and waited. He was cross, but he waited. Outside, a little bird sang in the almond tree.
pages.speech: “Grandma,” Rose called. “Please come and look.” Her little cousin held her hand tight and waited. He was cross, but he waited. Outside, a little bird sang in the almond tree.

pages.text: Grandma came in, wiping her hands. She put on her glasses, bent down and read the faded label slowly. She did not pick up the bottle. “This isn’t juice,” she said quietly. “It’s for cleaning the oven.” Then she knelt down and hugged them both, very tight.

pages.text: “Thank you for calling me, Rose,” said Grandma. “And thank you for waiting,” she told the little cousin. He gave a small, proud nod. Then Grandma looked at the low shelf. There were more bottles there, in all sorts of colours and shapes.

pages.text: Grandma stood on a sturdy step and moved every bottle up to the top shelf of the tall cupboard. Rose stood back and counted them out loud. “One, two, three, four, five, six, seven.” Seven bottles, all the way up high.

pages.text: Then Grandma closed the cupboard and locked it. She hung the key on a hook, high up by the door. Rose’s little cousin tipped his head right back and watched the key go up, and up, and up. It was much too high for him, and that was the point.

pages.text: Rose had an idea. She found a sheet of paper and a red crayon. Carefully, she drew a big red hand, with all five fingers spread wide. She held it up. “It means stop,” she said. “Stop, and ask first.”

pages.text: Her little cousin wanted to draw one too. His red hand had only four fingers and a smiley face in the middle. “Perfect,” said Grandma. They taped both hands on the cupboard door, side by side. The little one was a bit crooked, and nobody minded.

pages.text: Then Grandma washed her hands and took a jug of real orange juice from the fridge. She had squeezed it that morning. She poured three cups, and they all sat on the front step in the spring sunshine, side by side.
pages.speech: Then Grandma washed her hands and took a jug of real orange juice from the fridge. She had squeezed it that morning. She poured three cups, and they all sat on the front step in the spring sunshine, side by side.

pages.text: Rose’s little cousin held his cup in both hands. He looked at the juice. He looked at Grandma. “Grandma,” he said, “I’m asking first. Is this juice?” Grandma laughed so much that she nearly spilled hers. “Yes, my love,” she said. “This one is juice.” And it tasted of oranges and sunshine.

activity.title: Warning-Sign Detectives
activity.goal: Recognise the warning pictures on product labels.
materials: Two or three of your own closed cleaning products (held only by the grown-up)

steps.caption: The grown-up holds. Hands behind your back.
Find a warning picture. Point, don’t touch.
Draw a red hand for the cupboard.

activity.safety: Only the grown-up holds the products, keeps them closed, and puts them back up high straight afterwards. The child never holds, opens or smells them. If there is an accident, call your local emergency number.
activity.forAdult: In the story, Rose stops her little cousin from opening a bottle that looks exactly like juice. She does not touch it, she thinks about where it is, and she calls her grandmother, who reads the label and puts every bottle up high. The lesson for the child is simple: never taste or open a bottle, a box or a pill you do not know. Leave it where it is, and ask a grown-up first. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists keeping harmful household products out of reach among the safety goals for children of six to eight, and the American Academy of Pediatrics notes that most poisonings happen when caregivers are at home but not paying attention. So the grown-up’s part matters just as much: keep cleaning products and medicines closed, in their own bottles, never in drink bottles, and up high or locked away. In this activity the child learns to notice the warning pictures that many products carry, often a black picture inside a red-edged diamond. Take two or three closed products down yourself and hold them at the child’s eye level. The child keeps their hands behind their back and points to every warning picture they can find. Before you start, ask them to guess how many there will be; afterwards, count together. Then put everything straight back up high and close the cupboard while the child watches. Finish by drawing a red hand for the cupboard door, like Rose’s, and ask the child to explain what it means. Praise careful looking and asking first, not being “clever”. Keep the tone calm: the aim is a good habit, not fear. If you ever think a child has swallowed or touched a household product, call your local poison information centre or emergency number at once. Do not wait for signs, do not try to make the child sick, and keep the product with you so you can read out its label.
activity.inClass: Never bring real products into the classroom. The teacher shows large photographs of warning pictures on labels instead. Children find and count them in pairs, then each child draws a red-hand sign for a cupboard at home and explains to their partner what it means.
